items.question: What worldly reality is marked by freedom from the absence of mind?
premises: Mind and its absence are referenced
A state fully freed is indicated
This state is called a worldly reality and sign
items.inference: Freedom from the mere absence of mind is characterized as a worldly-level reality.
uncertainties: The exact syntactic relation among the compounds is compressed and ambiguous.
items.plain_english: That which is fully freed from the absence of mind is said to be a sign of worldly reality.

items.question: How is knowledge beyond mind and thought determined as ineffable?
premises: Mind and related factors are transcended
Knowledge is described as unthought
This knowledge is determined as ineffable
items.inference: True knowledge, unthought and beyond mind, is ascertained as ineffable.
uncertainties: The compound boundaries in avācya-jñāna-nirṇayam allow slight interpretive variation.
items.plain_english: Knowledge unthought by mind and so forth is determined to be ineffable knowledge.

items.question: What distinguishes the moving state from the characteristic mark of liberation?
premises: A moving state is explicitly named
An unmoving state is contrasted with it
The unmoving state is called the mark of liberation
items.inference: Liberation is characterized by unmoving steadiness rather than restless movement.
items.plain_english: The moving condition is thus described, while the unmoving is the characteristic of liberation.

items.question: Under what condition does the mind become unmoving and beyond itself?
premises: A state beyond mind is posited
The mind becomes determined
Determination results in unmoving steadiness
items.inference: When the mind is determined in a state beyond mind, it becomes unmoving.
uncertainties: The phrase citta-atītaṃ may qualify the mind or the resulting state.
items.plain_english: When the mind becomes determined as beyond mind, it becomes unmoving.

rows.grounds: related to inner practice; form uncertain

items.question: Why is a mind absorbed in yogic spirituality not an accomplishing characteristic?
premises: A yogic-spiritual mental orientation is negated
It is not an accomplishing characteristic
The negation is emphatically stated
items.inference: Mere yogic or spiritual mental absorption does not constitute the accomplishing mark sought.
uncertainties: The forms adhyāta and cittaḥ are non-standard or compressed in this text.
items.plain_english: It is not a mind absorbed in yoga and spiritual practice, nor is it an accomplishing characteristic.

items.question: Why can the ultimate reality not be located outside, inside, or in beginning, middle, and end?
premises: External and internal locations are negated
Position in beginning, middle, and end is negated
No spatial or sequential locus applies
items.inference: The reality in question transcends all spatial and sequential determinations.
uncertainties: The sequence bahir antam antaḥ sthaṃ is syntactically compressed.
items.plain_english: It is not outside or inside, nor situated within, nor located in beginning, middle, or end.

items.question: Why is the ultimate reality not identical with intellect, ego, mind, or sense faculties?
premises: Intellect is negated as its identity
Ego is negated as its identity
Mind and sense faculties are negated as its identity
items.inference: The reality in question is none of the inner instruments or sense faculties.
uncertainties: The form mana-indriyaḥ is compressed and may imply mind and senses together.
items.plain_english: It is not intellect, not ego, not mind or sense faculty.

items.question: How is the knowable reality distinguished from thought while ruling the time of knowing?
premises: The reality is not mere thought
It is to be known and understood
It is described as ruling the time of what is to be known
items.inference: The knowable reality transcends thought and governs the occasion of knowing.
uncertainties: The compound jñātavya-kāla-śāsanaḥ is interpretively dense.
items.plain_english: It is not thought; rather, it is to be known, the ruler of the time of what is to be known.

items.question: What hidden distinction is revealed in knowing the true nature of liberation?
premises: The true nature of liberation is to be known
A hidden distinction exists
That distinction is revealed
items.inference: Knowing liberation's true nature reveals a previously hidden distinction.
uncertainties: The referent of gupta-bheda is not explicitly specified.
items.plain_english: The true nature of liberation is to be known, as the hidden distinction is revealed.

items.question: Why is knowledge always declared to be without conceptualization in this exposition?
premises: Knowledge is described as without conceptualization
This quality is said to be constant
The exposition of knowledge declares this
items.inference: The teaching defines true knowledge as perpetually non-conceptual.
items.plain_english: Knowledge is always declared to be without conceptualization; this is stated in the exposition of knowledge.

items.question: What role do placements in moon, sun, and fire circles play in concentration practices?
premises: Concentration and placement are mentioned
Moon, sun, and fire circles are specified
These form a structured practice context
items.inference: The verse refers to concentrative placements within lunar, solar, and fiery circles.
uncertainties: The exact technical practice implied by the compound chain is not fully explicit.
items.plain_english: Concentration involves supports and placements in the circles of moon, sun, and fire.

items.question: Why are all such practices declared to be conceptual constructions rather than non-conceptual reality?
premises: All those practices are referred to
They are declared to be imagination or construction
Non-conceptuality is contrasted with otherness
items.inference: The cited practices are classified as conceptual constructions, unlike the non-conceptual state.
uncertainties: The contrast between tathā and anyathā is terse and open to nuance.
items.plain_english: All of these are declared to be conceptual constructions; the non-conceptual is otherwise.

items.question: How can the all-pervading reality be attained through methods devoid of accomplished sequence?
premises: The reality is described as all-pervading
A question is raised about attainment
The methods lack an accomplished sequence
items.inference: An all-pervading reality cannot be reached through practices lacking a perfected sequence.
uncertainties: The verse is rhetorical and its implied answer is unstated.
items.plain_english: How could the all-pervading be theirs, when it is devoid of an accomplished sequence?

items.question: Why do those situated in cyclic existence fail to reach the supreme state?
premises: Some remain situated in cyclic existence
They do not go to the supreme state
Their worldly situation is emphasized
items.inference: Abiding in cyclic existence prevents attainment of the supreme state.
items.plain_english: Those who remain situated here in cyclic existence do not reach the supreme state.

rows.grounds: devoid of or released from; form uncertain

items.question: How does freedom from the two bonds relate to the bondage of merit and demerit?
premises: A pair of bonds is identified
Freedom from this pair is stated
Merit and demerit are named as bondage
items.inference: Release from the two bonds involves release from the binding force of merit and demerit.
uncertainties: The form vinirūpaḥ is unusual and may be a textual variant.
items.plain_english: One is freed from the pair of bonds, namely the bondage of merit and demerit.

items.question: How can yogins progress when the mind is caught in a blinding bond?
premises: The mind is bound by a blinding fetter
A question is raised about movement
Yogins are the subjects in question
items.inference: A mind trapped in a blinding bond obstructs the yogins' progress.
uncertainties: The metaphorical sense of andha-pāśa is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: When the mind is in a blinding bond, where can the yogins go?

items.question: What consequence follows from being bound by that fetter for the accumulation of karma?
premises: One is bound by that bond
Being bound leads to experience
The accumulated store of karma is experienced
items.inference: Bondage by that fetter causes one to undergo the accumulated results of karma.
items.plain_english: Bound by that bond, one experiences the accumulation of karma.

items.question: Why are merit and demerit identified as the bondage of the three worlds?
premises: Merit and demerit form a pair
This pair is singled out
It is called the bondage of the three worlds
items.inference: The duality of merit and demerit binds beings within the three worlds.
uncertainties: The syntax linking yaḥ asau to the pair is compressed.
items.plain_english: Merit and demerit, those two, are the bondage of the three worlds.

items.question: In what way are merit and demerit declared to be twofold?
premises: Merit and demerit are named as a pair
They are explicitly declared
Their nature is described as twofold
items.inference: The pair of merit and demerit is taught as having a twofold character.
uncertainties: The forms dharmā and adharmā are non-standard for a dual subject.
items.plain_english: Merit and demerit, the two, are declared to be twofold.

items.question: Where is the true nature born of the inner self established for yogins?
premises: A true nature arises from the inner self
This concerns yogins specifically
That nature is established
items.inference: For yogins, the true nature born of the inner self is firmly established.
uncertainties: The subject of saṃsthitaḥ is implied rather than explicit.
items.plain_english: The true nature born of the inner self is established indeed in yogins.

rows.grounds: in the inner or spiritual domain

items.question: Why is the condition of merit and demerit always located in the inner domain?
premises: Merit and demerit are considered together
Their condition is located in the inner domain
This location is said to be constant
items.inference: The abiding of merit and demerit is always situated within the inner sphere.
items.plain_english: In the inner domain indeed, the condition of merit and demerit always abides.

rows.grounds: fetters or bonds; lexical sense uncertain

items.question: What liberation occurs when merit and demerit are exhausted and destroyed?
premises: Merit and demerit undergo destruction and exhaustion
Liberation is said to occur
Release is from all binding factors
items.inference: When merit and demerit are exhausted, one is liberated from all bonds.
uncertainties: The word dhanaiḥ is unusual here and may mean bonds rather than wealth.
items.plain_english: When merit and demerit are destroyed and exhausted, one is liberated from all bonds.

items.question: Who declares this investigation into merit and demerit as part of the knowledge exposition?
premises: An investigation of merit and demerit is presented
This investigation is declared
The declarers are expositors of knowledge
items.inference: The expositors of knowledge declare this analysis of merit and demerit.
items.plain_english: This investigation of merit and demerit has been declared by the expositors of knowledge.

items.question: Why is consciousness not wholly ignorance when it is described as devoid of knowledge?
premises: A conscious agent is identified
Ignorance is negated as total
Consciousness is described as devoid of knowledge
items.inference: Even when lacking knowledge, consciousness is not to be equated entirely with ignorance.
uncertainties: The syntax of sa cetā ajñāna na sarvaḥ is archaic and compressed.
items.plain_english: That conscious one is not entirely ignorance; consciousness is devoid of knowledge.
